info.name: DX ControlPlane - Onboarding E2E Copy
info.description:
End-to-end onboarding flow for the DX Control Plane, in the order the requests appear.

1. **Sign in** - password-grant logins for the requester, the COS Admin and the consumer.
2. **Organisation onboarding** - the requester submits an organisation create request; the
   COS Admin lists the pending queue and approves it; the requester refreshes their token to
   pick up the newly granted `org_admin` + `provider` roles and the `organisation_id` claim.
3. **Catalogue** - the new org admin publishes an asset.
4. **Access request** - the consumer requests access; the org admin approves it, creating an
   active policy; the consumer verifies the access.
5. **Auditing** - reads all of the above back through the activity API to prove each write was
   audited.
6. **Teardown** - deletes the policy and then the asset.

Ids are chained automatically through collection variables (`org_request_id`, `org_id`,
`item_id`, `access_request_id`, `policy_id`) - run the folders top to bottom in the Collection
Runner and nothing needs to be pasted by hand.

**Auditing (folder 04)** is checked *once, at the end* rather than after every request. Audit
rows are published to RabbitMQ from `addBodyEndHandler` - after the response has been written -
and inserted by a downstream consumer, so reading the activity API immediately after a write
races that consumer; and since the API is filterable and paginated, one call per actor covers
the whole trail. There is more than one call only because visibility is role-scoped: a consumer
sees just their own rows, an org admin their organisation's, a COS Admin everything. Each check
re-sends itself until the row appears (`audit_retry_max` x `audit_retry_delay_ms`), which needs
the Collection Runner or Newman - `setNextRequest` does nothing on a single send.

**Teardown (folder 05)** has a required order: `DELETE /cat/item` refuses with 409 while any
ACTIVE policy references the item, so the policy is soft-deleted first. The 409 is asserted
rather than avoided, so the guard is covered too.

**Configuration** lives entirely in the environment - the collection itself contains no host,
credential or payload literal, so the same collection runs unchanged against every
deployment. Two environments ship with it:

- `env-onboarding-local` - working values for the docker-compose stack.
- `env-onboarding-template` - duplicate this once per deployment and fill the twelve
  `<angle-bracket>` placeholders. Everything without a placeholder already has a usable
  default and only needs touching if you want different fixture data.

Only these twelve are deployment-specific: `base_url`, `acl_url`, `kc_url`, `realm`,
`client_id`, `client_secret`, and the three username/password pairs. On a deployed
environment the control plane and the ACL/APD API sit behind the *same* host and differ only
by path, so `base_url` and `acl_url` are usually identical - they are split only because the
local stack exposes them on ports 8080 and 8444. Leave `client_secret` empty for a public
client; if the client is confidential, fill it in and enable the disabled `client_secret`
row in the body of each login request.

**Re-running:** a user may hold only one pending or granted org create request, and the org
name and manager e-mail must be unique platform-wide. `unique_run_suffix=true` appends a
timestamp to the org name, manager e-mail and item name so repeated runs do not collide - but
folder 01 still needs a *fresh* `requester_user` each time. Set `unique_run_suffix=false` to
send the literal values from the environment.

**Prerequisites**

- `requester_user` is a *fresh* Keycloak user with a password, no organisation and no
  `org_admin` role. The seeded `orgadmin` user in `dev/keycloak/realm-iudx.json` already has
  that role, so it cannot drive this flow - create a new one.
- `consumer_user` holds the `consumer` role (the seeded `consumer1` does).
- The client named by `client_id` has direct access grants enabled (`postman-client` does).
- KYC: the org-create and join routes are guarded by `kycVerification(kycRequired)`. The
  config flag `kycRequired` is `false` in the example and dev configs; if you turn it on, the
  requester must be KYC verified first.
- The dev realm ships without protocol mappers, so `organisation_id` is not in the token. The
  "Refresh requester token" test therefore only asserts the roles, and `org_id` is picked up
  by the "Confirm org membership" request that follows it. Add a user-attribute mapper for
  `organisation_id` if you want the claim in the token as well.

request.description: Same endpoint as above, but an `org_admin` reads at organisation level, so the server adds an `org_id` filter. The `org_id` stored on a row comes *only* from the `organisation_id` token claim - there is no database fallback - so on a realm without that protocol mapper every row is written with a null `org_id` and this query returns nothing. The assertions are therefore gated on `org_claim_mapped`; set it to `true` once the mapper exists, and the request logs a skip notice until then.

item.description:
Verifies that the six writes above actually landed in `activity_audit_log`, by reading them back through the activity API.

**Run this folder once, at the end - not after every request.** Auditing is asynchronous (published to RabbitMQ once the response has been written, then inserted by a consumer), so an immediate read races the consumer; and the activity API is filterable and paginated, so a single call per actor can assert the whole trail. Each request below retries itself up to `audit_retry_max` times with `audit_retry_delay_ms` between attempts - which needs the Collection Runner or Newman, since `setNextRequest` is a no-op on a single send.

Visibility is role-scoped, which is why there is more than one call: a consumer sees only their own rows, an org admin only their organisation's, and only a COS Admin sees everything.

Delete item - blocked by active policy (Org Admin)

exec: pm.test("delete is blocked while a policy is active", function () {

request.description: Expected to fail with 409. This is the guard that makes the rest of this folder necessary: the item cannot be removed while a policy references it. Skip this request if you only want the happy path.

exec: pm.test("active policy found for the item", function () {
pm.expect(match, "no ACTIVE policy for item " + wanted).to.be.an("object");

request.description: The approval in folder 03 created the policy server-side, so its id was never returned to the client. Lists the policies on the caller's assets and stores `policy_id` for the ACTIVE one matching `asset.itemId`. Add `policyType=ACCESS_REQUEST_APPROVED` to see only approval-created policies.

A soft delete despite the name - the policy moves from `ACTIVE` to `DELETE` along with its access rules, and the record is retained for audit. Access granted through it is revoked immediately and it cannot be reactivated; a new policy has to be created instead. The caller must be the asset's provider or an org admin of its organisation, and the policy must currently be ACTIVE.
The mirror of the check at the end of folder 03 - the consumer that was granted access should no longer have it.
Succeeds now that no ACTIVE policy points at the item. The item is backed up before removal and a `Delete` audit row is written.

item.description:
Removes what the run created, in the only order the server accepts: the policy first, then the asset.

`DELETE /cat/item` checks `hasActivePolicies(assetId)` before it does anything and fails with **409 Conflict - "Item cannot be deleted as it has active policies"** while the grant from folder 03 is still ACTIVE. The first request here asserts that 409 deliberately, so the guard itself is covered; then the policy is soft-deleted (`ACTIVE` -> `DELETE`, rules included, record kept for traceability) and the same delete succeeds.

Both deletes are audited too - they add `Delete` rows - so run folder 04 before this one if you want its assertions to see the trail as it was.

item.name: 06 - Other servers
item.description: The servers the onboarding story does not otherwise touch - one call each at the file server and OGC, three at the community layer (its health route plus the public read of each product it mounts) and two at the sandbox (health, then an unauthenticated call to a real API route): the same calls main/e2e.py's community and sandbox checks make. Each server runs as its own phase and only where it is enabled in config; the file and OGC reads address the item this run onboarded, so they run after the data has been published. Every one of them is a read: nothing here needs tearing down.

request.description: The token-optional read main/e2e.py's community check makes: /discussion/tags/popular is an http_bearer_header_public route, so it answers an anonymous caller with real data. That is the positive half of the community check - it proves the discussion router is mounted (a deployment whose ACTIVATED_SERVICES omits it answers 404, not 401) and that the product is reading its own database. Deliberately unauthenticated: an authenticated request inserts a users row that no route deletes, and the public bearer returns early before that code is reached. Nothing is created.

item.name: Sandbox - health, the route that sits outside the auth middleware

exec: pm.test("HTTP 200 - the service is up and serving", function () {

request.description: The health call main/e2e.py's sandbox check makes. The handler is a literal {"status": "ok", "version": …}, so the body is asserted rather than the status alone - a 200 carrying "degraded" is a pass by status and a failure in fact. This proves the process is up and serving; it says nothing about auth, because the route is registered outside authMiddleware, which is what the request after it is for. No token, nothing created.
